questions.title: Why can binary floating-point make 0.1 + 0.2 differ from 0.3 in Java?
explanation: double stores nearby binary fractions rather than exact decimal fractions. Use BigDecimal constructed from decimal text when exact base-10 arithmetic and rounding rules matter.

questions.title: How does binary numeric promotion affect arithmetic on byte and short values?
explanation: Arithmetic promotes byte, short, and char operands to int, so the result usually needs an explicit narrowing conversion before assignment to a smaller type.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Conversions and Contexts

questions.title: Why can compound assignment compile when the equivalent simple assignment does not?
explanation: A compound assignment includes an implicit conversion back to the left-hand type, while the expanded arithmetic expression normally has the promoted type and needs an explicit cast.

questions.title: What does integer division do when either operand is negative?
explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero, and the remainder has the dividend sign. Use floorDiv and floorMod when mathematical floor semantics are required.

questions.title: What happens when an int calculation overflows?
explanation: Integral overflow wraps in two-complement arithmetic without an exception. Use exact arithmetic helpers such as Math.addExact when overflow must be detected.

questions.title: Why is char insufficient for representing every Unicode character?
explanation: char stores one UTF-16 code unit, while supplementary Unicode characters require a surrogate pair. Code-point APIs are required for character-aware traversal.

questions.title: How does left-to-right operand evaluation influence side effects?
explanation: Java evaluates operand expressions left to right, so earlier side effects are visible to later operands. Clear code should still avoid combining multiple mutations in one expression.

questions.title: What is the difference between short-circuit and non-short-circuit boolean operators?
explanation: && and || skip the right operand when the result is already known; & and | on booleans evaluate both operands, which can trigger side effects or exceptions.

questions.title: Why can the conditional operator produce an unexpected numeric type?
explanation: The conditional operator applies detailed numeric and reference typing rules to its second and third operands; boxing, unboxing, and promotion can change the inferred result type.

questions.title: What prints when a post-increment value is assigned back to the same variable?
explanation: The postfix expression yields the old value after performing the increment, then the assignment writes that old value back, so x remains 4.

questions.title: Why does Integer identity comparison sometimes appear to work for small values?
explanation: Boxing may reuse cached wrapper instances for a required small range, but identity is not numeric equality. Compare wrapper values with equals or unbox them.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Conversions and Contexts

questions.title: How can unboxing a nullable wrapper fail?
explanation: Unboxing invokes the wrapper value conversion; a null reference therefore throws NullPointerException. Keep absence explicit or validate before unboxing.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Conversions and Contexts

questions.title: Why can an overloaded call become ambiguous when passed null?
explanation: null is compatible with every reference type, so unrelated overload parameter types may be equally specific. A cast or a clearer API resolves the ambiguity.

questions.title: How do primitive widening and boxing compete during overload resolution?
explanation: Method invocation prefers applicable fixed-arity methods using primitive widening before considering boxing and then variable arity, so nearby overloads can select unexpectedly.

questions.title: Why does a generic method sometimes infer Object instead of a narrower type?
explanation: Inference must satisfy constraints from every argument and the target context. Conflicting argument types can force their least useful common supertype.

questions.title: What is a bridge method and why does the compiler generate one?
explanation: Type erasure can change an overriding method signature, so the compiler emits a synthetic bridge that preserves polymorphism and delegates to the typed implementation.

questions.title: Why is List<String> not a subtype of List<Object>?
explanation: Generic types are invariant because allowing that assignment would permit inserting a non-String into a list whose actual element type is String.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Types, Values, and Variables

questions.title: What information can a reifiable type preserve at runtime?
explanation: A reifiable type has enough runtime representation for operations such as instanceof; raw types, non-generic types, and unbounded wildcard forms are common examples.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Types, Values, and Variables

questions.title: Why can reflection see a generic signature even though Java uses erasure?
explanation: Class files may retain generic signature metadata for reflection and tooling, while JVM execution and casts still use erased runtime types.

questions.title: What does this wildcard capture helper make possible?
explanation: The helper gives the unknown wildcard element type a temporary name, allowing a value read from the list to be written back safely.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Types, Values, and Variables

questions.title: How does a canonical record constructor differ from a compact constructor?
explanation: A canonical constructor declares the full component parameter list and assigns fields; a compact constructor omits both and lets the compiler perform final assignments after validation.

questions.title: Why should a record containing a mutable list make a defensive copy?
explanation: Record fields are final references, not deeply immutable values. Copying the list prevents callers from mutating record state through an external alias.

questions.title: How does an enum guarantee a controlled instance set?
explanation: Enum constants are the only direct instances exposed by the declaration, and construction is controlled by the runtime, supporting identity-safe singleton constants.

questions.title: When is EnumMap more appropriate than HashMap?
explanation: EnumMap stores keys from one enum type compactly in natural declaration order and rejects null keys, making it efficient and explicit for closed key domains.

questions.title: What determines whether an annotation is visible through reflection?
explanation: Its retention policy controls whether it exists only in source, in the class file, or at runtime; only runtime-retained annotations are available to reflection.

questions.title: Are annotations inherited from interfaces or methods automatically?
explanation: The Inherited meta-annotation affects class-level lookup through a superclass chain only; it does not automatically propagate interface or method annotations.

questions.title: Why can reflective access fail even for a public member?
explanation: The declaring package may not be exported or opened to the caller module, and access checks still consider the member, class, package, and module boundaries.

questions.title: When is MethodHandle preferable to reflective Method.invoke?
explanation: Method handles provide strongly typed invocation shapes, composition, and JVM optimization opportunities, while reflection is often simpler for occasional metadata-driven calls.

questions.title: What does ClassValue solve for framework metadata caches?
explanation: ClassValue associates computed data with each Class while allowing lifecycle behavior aligned with class unloading, avoiding common strong-key cache leaks.

questions.title: Why does this enum comparison safely tolerate null only on one side?
explanation: Calling equals on a nullable reference can fail, while comparing an enum constant with == is identity-based and safely returns false for null.

code.snippet:
Status status = loadStatus();
boolean active = status == Status.ACTIVE;

questions.title: Why does String.strip differ from String.trim?
explanation: strip uses Unicode whitespace semantics, whereas trim removes characters at or below a legacy code-point threshold. strip is usually better for international text.

questions.title: How can String.intern affect memory and identity?
explanation: intern returns a canonical pool reference, enabling identity sharing but potentially increasing pool pressure and coupling logic to global canonicalization.

questions.title: When should StringBuilder capacity be sized in advance?
explanation: A reasonable estimate reduces backing-array growth and copying for large predictable output, but over-allocation wastes memory and should be guided by measurements.

questions.title: Why is repeated string concatenation in a loop potentially expensive?
explanation: Each immutable concatenation can create new intermediate storage; a StringBuilder accumulates changes in one mutable buffer when the compiler cannot optimize the pattern.

questions.title: What is catastrophic backtracking in a regular expression?
explanation: Nested ambiguous quantifiers can make a backtracking engine explore exponentially many paths on hostile input. Bound input, simplify the pattern, or use possessive constructs.

questions.title: How do matches, lookingAt, and find differ in Matcher?
explanation: matches requires the entire region, lookingAt starts at the region beginning, and find searches for the next matching subsequence.

questions.title: Why should Pattern instances often be reused?
explanation: Compiling a regular expression parses and builds matcher machinery; a compiled immutable Pattern can be safely reused while Matcher instances remain per-operation.

questions.title: Why should BigDecimal values usually be created from strings?
explanation: A decimal string preserves the intended base-10 value, while constructing from double captures that binary floating-point value and may expose a long decimal expansion.

questions.title: How do BigDecimal.equals and compareTo differ?
explanation: equals considers both value and scale, while compareTo compares numerical value. Thus 2.0 and 2.00 compare as zero but are not equal.

questions.title: What does this text-block indentation produce?
explanation: Incidental indentation shared by the closing delimiter and content is removed, preserving a readable source layout without embedding all leading source spaces.

questions.title: Why is ArrayDeque usually preferred over Stack?
explanation: ArrayDeque provides efficient stack and queue operations without Stack legacy synchronization and Vector inheritance; null elements are deliberately unsupported.

questions.title: How does PriorityQueue order iteration versus removal?
explanation: The head follows priority order, but iteration is not sorted. Repeated poll operations are required to consume elements by priority.

questions.title: When is IdentityHashMap appropriate?
explanation: It compares keys by reference identity instead of equals, fitting topology transforms or object-graph tracking; it violates normal Map equality expectations for business keys.

questions.title: What cleanup behavior can WeakHashMap provide?
explanation: Entries may disappear after keys become weakly reachable, which can help attach auxiliary data without owning key lifetime; collection timing is nondeterministic.

questions.title: Why is CopyOnWriteArrayList good for reads but costly for writes?
explanation: Reads use stable snapshots without locking, while each mutation copies the backing array. It suits small, rarely changed listener lists rather than write-heavy data.

questions.title: How does ConcurrentSkipListMap differ from ConcurrentHashMap?
explanation: It maintains sorted keys and navigation operations with logarithmic expected costs, whereas ConcurrentHashMap emphasizes unordered high-throughput key access.

questions.title: What does NavigableMap.floorEntry return?
explanation: It returns the greatest key-value entry whose key is less than or equal to the target, or null when no such key exists.

questions.title: Why can Collections.binarySearch return a negative number?
explanation: A negative result encodes the insertion point as -(point)-1, allowing callers to preserve ordering without performing a second search.

questions.title: How does BitSet reduce storage for dense boolean indexes?
explanation: It packs flags into machine words and supplies bulk logical operations, often using far less memory than boxed Boolean collections.

questions.title: What ordering does this priority queue produce?
explanation: The reverse-order comparator makes the greatest number the head, so poll returns 9 before 4 and 1.

questions.title: What is the purpose of SequencedCollection?
explanation: It gives ordered collections a uniform first, last, and reversed view API, reducing type-specific code for encounter-order operations.

questions.title: How does a reversed collection view differ from a copied reversal?
explanation: A reversed view presents opposite encounter order over the same underlying collection, so permitted changes remain connected rather than creating an independent snapshot.

questions.title: Why can a TreeSet silently reject a value unequal by equals?
explanation: TreeSet uniqueness follows compareTo or its Comparator. If comparison returns zero, the set treats values as the same element regardless of equals.

questions.title: When should Arrays.mismatch be used?
explanation: It efficiently locates the first differing position between arrays, which helps implement comparison, diagnostics, and prefix checks without a manual scan.

questions.title: How does Collections.rotate transform a list?
explanation: It shifts each element by a modular distance, wrapping at the ends; positive distance moves elements toward higher indexes.

questions.title: What does a Spliterator characteristic communicate?
explanation: Characteristics such as ORDERED, DISTINCT, SORTED, SIZED, and IMMUTABLE let traversal consumers select valid optimizations without changing semantics.

questions.title: Why does a good Spliterator trySplit matter for parallel streams?
explanation: Balanced splitting creates enough similarly sized tasks for worker utilization; poor splitting leaves parallel overhead without useful load distribution.

questions.title: How can a custom collector remain correct in parallel?
explanation: Its supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher, and characteristics must form a compatible reduction whose grouping and ordering semantics survive partitioned execution.

questions.title: What is the cost of maintaining insertion order in LinkedHashMap?
explanation: It adds a linked ordering structure and related update work, trading some memory and mutation cost for predictable encounter or access order.

questions.title: How can LinkedHashMap implement a bounded LRU-style cache?
explanation: Access-order mode moves read entries toward the newest end, and removeEldestEntry can evict the oldest entry after insertion; external synchronization may still be needed.

questions.title: Why are streams described as lazy?
explanation: Intermediate operations build a pipeline and normally do no traversal until a terminal operation requests results, enabling fusion and short-circuiting.

questions.title: Why can reusing a consumed Stream fail?
explanation: A stream represents a single traversal pipeline; after a terminal operation it is closed to further operations and may throw IllegalStateException.

questions.title: How does mapMulti differ from flatMap?
explanation: mapMulti emits zero or more results through a consumer without allocating a new stream per input, which can be useful for small expansions.

questions.title: When does takeWhile differ from filter?
explanation: takeWhile stops at the first predicate failure in encounter order, while filter evaluates the full stream and keeps every matching element.

questions.title: Why can distinct be expensive on a parallel ordered stream?
explanation: It is a stateful barrier that must track seen values while preserving encounter order. Removing ordering only when semantics allow can improve parallel execution.

questions.title: How do groupingBy and partitioningBy differ?
explanation: partitioningBy always creates boolean groups, while groupingBy derives arbitrary keys and supports richer classification maps.

questions.title: What problem do downstream collectors solve?
explanation: They let each group perform another reduction, such as mapping, filtering, counting, or summarizing, without materializing every grouped element first.

questions.title: When is Optional.orElseGet preferable to orElse?
explanation: orElse evaluates its fallback eagerly even when a value exists; orElseGet invokes the supplier only when the optional is empty.

questions.title: Why should Optional generally not be used as every field type?
explanation: Optional was designed primarily as a return-value signal. Pervasive fields can complicate serialization, frameworks, allocation, and domain invariants.

questions.title: What does this stream pipeline return?
explanation: The pipeline stops once it finds the first even number after filtering, so the result is Optional containing 8 and later elements need not be tested.

questions.title: When should ReentrantLock be chosen over synchronized?
explanation: It provides capabilities such as timed or interruptible acquisition, multiple conditions, and explicit fairness policy, at the cost of manual finally-based release.

questions.title: How does ReentrantReadWriteLock help read-heavy state?
explanation: It permits concurrent readers while serializing writers, but bookkeeping and contention can make it slower than one lock for short or write-heavy operations.

questions.title: What is an optimistic read in StampedLock?
explanation: It reads without taking a traditional read lock and then validates a stamp; failed validation requires retrying under a stable lock.

questions.title: How does Semaphore model a bounded resource?
explanation: Permits represent concurrent capacity. Callers acquire before use and release in finally, limiting access independently of the number of requesting threads.

questions.title: When is CountDownLatch useful?
explanation: It lets threads wait until a fixed set of one-time events completes; unlike a barrier, its count cannot be reset for another phase.

questions.title: How does CyclicBarrier coordinate phases?
explanation: A fixed group waits at the barrier until all arrive, then the barrier resets for another round and can run a barrier action.

questions.title: What problem does Phaser solve beyond CountDownLatch?
explanation: Phaser supports reusable phases and dynamic party registration, fitting workflows whose participants change across coordinated stages.

questions.title: When is Exchanger useful?
explanation: It pairs two threads at a synchronization point so each hands one object to the other, useful for buffer handoff or paired pipeline stages.

questions.title: How does SynchronousQueue provide backpressure?
explanation: It has no storage capacity; each put must rendezvous with a take, directly coupling producer throughput to consumer readiness.

questions.title: Why must a lock be released in finally?
explanation: An exception between acquisition and release would otherwise leave the lock held and can permanently block other threads.

questions.title: What is the difference between execute and submit on ExecutorService?
explanation: execute runs a task without a result handle, while submit returns a Future that captures completion, cancellation, result, or failure.

questions.title: Why can exceptions from submitted tasks appear to vanish?
explanation: submit stores task failure in the Future; if nobody calls get or observes completion, the exception may never reach normal uncaught-exception reporting.

questions.title: How should a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor rejection policy be selected?
explanation: Choose whether to fail, block elsewhere, run on the caller, or discard based on workload semantics; rejection is an overload contract, not just an error detail.

questions.title: What does CompletableFuture thenCompose prevent?
explanation: It flattens an asynchronous function returning another stage, avoiding a nested CompletionStage of CompletionStage.

questions.title: How do handle and exceptionally differ in CompletableFuture?
explanation: exceptionally recovers only from failure, while handle observes both a value and an exception and can transform either outcome.

questions.title: Why can blocking the common ForkJoinPool cause starvation?
explanation: Workers are sized for work-stealing computation; unmanaged blocking removes workers from useful work and can delay dependent tasks.

questions.title: How does ForkJoinPool work stealing improve utilization?
explanation: Idle workers take tasks from other workers queues, balancing recursively divided work without a single central scheduling bottleneck.

questions.title: When should ForkJoinTask use managedBlock?
explanation: A task that must block can notify the pool through managedBlock so it may compensate with another worker and preserve parallelism.

questions.title: What cancellation guarantee does Future.cancel provide?
explanation: It attempts cancellation; interruption is cooperative and may be ignored, so task code must observe interruption and preserve consistent state.

questions.title: What does this CompletableFuture chain print?
explanation: thenApply transforms the completed value synchronously when possible, producing 42, and join returns it or wraps failure in CompletionException.

questions.title: What problem does structured concurrency address?
explanation: It treats related concurrent subtasks as one lexical unit, making lifetime, joining, cancellation, and error propagation easier to reason about.

questions.title: Why should preview Java APIs be isolated in production code?
explanation: Preview features can change or disappear and require explicit compiler and runtime flags, so a boundary limits migration and operational risk.

questions.title: How do scoped values differ from ThreadLocal?
explanation: Scoped values provide immutable context within a bounded dynamic scope and are designed for structured task inheritance without long-lived mutable thread state.

questions.title: Why does Thread.sleep not release an intrinsic lock?
explanation: sleep pauses the current thread but does not change monitor ownership; wait releases the monitor while waiting and requires synchronized ownership.

questions.title: How does park differ from sleep?
explanation: LockSupport park uses a permit-like mechanism and may return spuriously; it integrates with synchronizer implementations rather than promising a precise delay.

questions.title: What should happen when a blocking Java operation is interrupted?
explanation: Code should normally propagate InterruptedException or restore the interrupt flag after cleanup so higher layers can honor cancellation.

questions.title: Why is Thread.stop unsafe?
explanation: It can asynchronously release monitors while protected invariants are half-updated. Cooperative cancellation gives code controlled cleanup points.

questions.title: How do daemon threads affect JVM shutdown?
explanation: The JVM may exit when only daemon threads remain, so critical persistence or cleanup must not rely solely on daemon work finishing.

questions.title: What limits virtual-thread scalability in a real service?
explanation: Database connections, remote quotas, memory, CPU, file descriptors, and pinned blocking sections still require explicit capacity and backpressure.

questions.title: What does this try-with-resources executor block guarantee?
explanation: The executor is closed at block exit, which waits for submitted tasks according to its close contract and makes task lifetime explicit.

questions.title: What does happens-before mean in the Java Memory Model?
explanation: If one action happens-before another, its effects are guaranteed visible and ordered to the later action; absence of that relation permits surprising observations.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Threads and Locks

questions.title: Why does volatile provide visibility but not make count++ atomic?
explanation: A volatile read and write are individually visible and ordered, but increment is a read-modify-write sequence that can interleave across threads.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Threads and Locks

questions.title: What safe-publication guarantees do final fields receive?
explanation: When construction does not leak this, properly initialized final fields receive special visibility guarantees after another thread obtains the object reference.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Threads and Locks

questions.title: What is double-checked locking missing without volatile?
explanation: Without volatile, publication can be reordered so another thread sees a non-null reference before constructor effects are safely visible.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Threads and Locks

questions.title: How does AtomicInteger compareAndSet support lock-free updates?
explanation: It conditionally writes only when the current value equals the expected value, allowing retry loops to coordinate without a mutual-exclusion lock.

questions.title: What is the ABA problem in compare-and-set algorithms?
explanation: A value can change from A to B and back to A, so equality alone hides intervening state changes; stamped or versioned references can detect them.

questions.title: When is LongAdder preferable to AtomicLong?
explanation: Under heavy concurrent updates, striped cells reduce contention for counters, but sum is not an atomic snapshot and per-update linearizability is weaker.

questions.title: What does a VarHandle provide?
explanation: It offers typed access modes for fields and array elements, including plain, opaque, acquire-release, volatile, and atomic operations.

questions.title: Why can false sharing reduce multicore performance?
explanation: Independent hot fields on the same cache line cause processors to invalidate each others caches, creating coherence traffic without logical sharing.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Threads and Locks

questions.title: Why can this loop fail to stop without proper synchronization?
explanation: The worker has a data race on running; the compiler or CPU need not make another threads write promptly visible. volatile establishes the required visibility.

source.title: Java Language Specification: Threads and Locks

questions.title: How does Path differ from File?
explanation: Path is the modern filesystem abstraction used by Files and provider APIs, with richer operations, links, attributes, and custom filesystem support.

questions.title: Why should Files.lines be used in try-with-resources?
explanation: The lazy stream holds an open file resource until the stream is closed, so deterministic closure is required even when traversal fails.

questions.title: What does an atomic file move guarantee?
explanation: When the provider supports it, observers see the path switch as one operation rather than a partially copied destination; support must be detected.

questions.title: How should temporary files be created safely?
explanation: Use Files.createTempFile with controlled permissions and cleanup rather than predictable names, which invite collisions and race attacks.

questions.title: What are the limitations of WatchService?
explanation: Events may be coalesced or overflowed and behavior varies by provider, so consumers must rescan after overflow and not treat it as a perfect audit log.

questions.title: When is a memory-mapped byte buffer useful?
explanation: It lets the operating system map file regions into memory for efficient random access, but mapping lifetime and unmapping behavior require care.

questions.title: How do flip and compact differ on a ByteBuffer?
explanation: flip prepares written bytes for reading by setting the limit and resetting position; compact preserves unread bytes and makes space for more input.

questions.title: Why must CharsetDecoder errors be handled explicitly?
explanation: Malformed or unmappable byte sequences require a reporting, replacement, or ignore policy; silent platform defaults can corrupt data.

questions.title: What advantage do scattering reads and gathering writes provide?
explanation: A channel can transfer data across several buffers in one operation, fitting protocols with separate headers and bodies while reducing copying.

questions.title: What state does this buffer have after flip?
explanation: Position becomes zero and limit becomes the previous position, so get reads exactly the bytes that were written.

questions.title: How does a Selector scale many socket channels?
explanation: One thread can wait for readiness across many non-blocking channels, avoiding one platform thread per mostly idle connection.

questions.title: What does asynchronous file I/O completion handling change?
explanation: The initiating thread does not wait for the operation; a Future or completion handler observes success and failure later.

questions.title: Why should Socket timeouts be set deliberately?
explanation: Without connection, read, and operation deadlines, a dependency or network fault can retain threads and capacity indefinitely.

questions.title: How does URI differ from URL in Java?
explanation: URI models and parses identifiers without requiring a protocol handler, while URL includes resource-access behavior and legacy equality pitfalls.

questions.title: What does HttpClient.Redirect control?
explanation: It determines whether redirects are never followed, followed for normal schemes, or always followed, making redirect trust a client policy.

questions.title: How does HTTP client body streaming avoid large buffering?
explanation: Body publishers and subscribers can transfer content incrementally, allowing backpressure-aware handling instead of materializing the full body.

questions.title: Why should an HttpClient instance be reused?
explanation: It can share connection pools and configuration, avoiding repeated setup and improving transport efficiency across requests.

questions.title: What does WebSocket backpressure require from Java code?
explanation: Demand must be requested and message processing kept bounded; receiving faster than consumption without limits can exhaust memory.

questions.title: How should an application validate TLS host identity?
explanation: Use the standard HTTPS client verification path and trusted certificates; disabling hostname checks converts encryption into an unauthenticated channel.

questions.title: What is asynchronous about this sendAsync call?
explanation: sendAsync returns a CompletableFuture immediately; response handling continues when headers and the selected body handler complete.

questions.title: When should Instant be stored instead of LocalDateTime?
explanation: Instant identifies a unique timeline point, while LocalDateTime has no offset or zone and can be ambiguous during clock changes.

questions.title: How do OffsetDateTime and ZonedDateTime differ?
explanation: OffsetDateTime stores a fixed UTC offset; ZonedDateTime also stores region rules that determine historical and future offset transitions.

questions.title: Why can parsing a local time during a daylight-saving overlap be ambiguous?
explanation: The same wall-clock value can occur twice with different offsets, so business rules must select an offset or retain the zone-aware result.

questions.title: How do Period and Duration model different quantities?
explanation: Period uses calendar units such as years, months, and days; Duration measures exact elapsed seconds and nanoseconds.

questions.title: What does Clock injection improve in tests?
explanation: Code can obtain time through a supplied Clock, allowing deterministic fixed or offset time without changing the system clock.

questions.title: Why is DateTimeFormatter immutable useful?
explanation: A configured formatter can be safely reused across threads, unlike mutable legacy formatting classes that require confinement or synchronization.

questions.title: How should Locale-sensitive case conversion be performed?
explanation: Pass the intended Locale explicitly; use Locale.ROOT for protocol identifiers so host default language rules cannot change behavior.

questions.title: Why should Collator be used for user-facing sort order?
explanation: Unicode code-point order is not natural language order. Collator applies locale-sensitive comparison levels and rules.

questions.title: What does ResourceBundle fallback provide?
explanation: It searches progressively less specific locale bundles and a base bundle, allowing translated overrides with shared defaults.

questions.title: What instant does this zone conversion preserve?
explanation: withZoneSameInstant changes the displayed local fields and offset while preserving the exact timeline moment.

code.snippet: ZonedDateTime india = meeting.withZoneSameInstant(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));

questions.title: How do MessageDigest and Mac serve different security purposes?
explanation: A digest detects accidental change without a secret; a MAC authenticates integrity using a shared secret and resists attacker recomputation.

questions.title: Why should password storage use a password-hashing function rather than SHA-256?
explanation: Password KDFs deliberately add salt and adjustable computational cost, making offline guessing more expensive than a fast general digest.

source.title: Secure Coding Guidelines for Java SE

questions.title: What is the role of KeyStore?
explanation: It stores and retrieves keys and certificates through provider-backed formats, while access controls and password handling remain application responsibilities.

questions.title: Why must AES-GCM nonces never repeat under one key?
explanation: Nonce reuse breaks GCM confidentiality and authentication guarantees, potentially exposing plaintext relationships and enabling forgeries.

questions.title: What does Signature verification establish?
explanation: It checks that data matches a signature under a public key, providing integrity and signer-key authenticity when the key itself is trusted.

questions.title: How does certificate-path validation differ from checking one signature?
explanation: Path validation builds trust through issuers and applies validity, constraints, revocation policy, and a configured trust anchor.

questions.title: Why should secrets not be stored in immutable String objects?
explanation: Strings cannot be wiped and may remain in memory; mutable character or byte arrays allow deliberate clearing after use, though copies must still be controlled.

source.title: Secure Coding Guidelines for Java SE

questions.title: What does a security provider supply?
explanation: A provider implements named cryptographic services and algorithms; callers should request standard algorithms and validate deployment provider capabilities.

questions.title: Why is deserializing untrusted Java objects dangerous?
explanation: Object graphs can trigger unexpected class behavior and resource consumption. Prefer constrained data formats or strict serialization filters and allowlists.

questions.title: What security property does this comparison need?
explanation: Authentication tags and secret values should use a constant-time comparison primitive where available to reduce timing leakage from early mismatch exits.

code.snippet: boolean valid = MessageDigest.isEqual(expectedTag, suppliedTag);

questions.title: What does an ObjectInputFilter limit?
explanation: It can reject deserialization based on classes, graph depth, references, array size, and bytes, reducing but not eliminating unsafe format risk.

questions.title: Why is serialVersionUID important for Serializable classes?
explanation: It identifies a serialization version; an incompatible stream and class version can fail, but matching IDs do not guarantee semantic compatibility.

questions.title: When should readResolve be treated cautiously?
explanation: It can replace a deserialized object, supporting canonical instances but also adding hidden execution and invariant complexity to deserialization.

questions.title: How can XML external entities create a server-side request risk?
explanation: An unsafe parser may resolve attacker-controlled external identifiers against files or networks. Disable external resolution and use secure parser settings.

source.title: Secure Coding Guidelines for Java SE

questions.title: Why should ProcessBuilder arguments remain separate strings?
explanation: Separate arguments avoid shell parsing and injection when no shell is invoked; adding a shell reintroduces quoting and metacharacter risks.

questions.title: How should a Java process avoid deadlock on child output?
explanation: Consume stdout and stderr concurrently or redirect them, because a child can block when an unread pipe buffer fills.

questions.title: What does ProcessHandle provide?
explanation: It exposes process identity, metadata, descendants, liveness, completion, and controlled termination without relying on platform-specific commands.

questions.title: Why should shutdown hooks be small and bounded?
explanation: Hooks run during JVM shutdown with uncertain ordering and limited time; blocking dependencies or deadlocks can prevent timely termination.

questions.title: When does Cleaner help, and what can it not guarantee?
explanation: Cleaner can provide a safety-net action when an object becomes phantom reachable, but timing is nondeterministic and explicit close remains required.

questions.title: What does this try-with-resources suppression behavior preserve?
explanation: The body exception remains primary while a close failure is attached as suppressed, retaining both causes without hiding the original failure.

questions.title: What triggers Java class initialization?
explanation: First active use such as invoking a static method, accessing a nonconstant static field, or constructing an instance initializes the class after its superclasses.

questions.title: Why can a class remain unusable after static initialization fails?
explanation: The first failure throws an initializer error; later active uses typically receive NoClassDefFoundError because initialization is marked erroneous.

questions.title: How do bootstrap, platform, and application class loaders relate?
explanation: They form the built-in delegation hierarchy for core runtime, platform modules, and application class path or module path classes.

questions.title: What creates class-loader identity conflicts in plugin systems?
explanation: The runtime type identity includes both binary class name and defining loader, so identical class bytes from sibling loaders are not assignment-compatible.

questions.title: What is a module readability edge?
explanation: It records that one module may access exported public types of another; requires directives and resolution establish the graph.

questions.title: How does requires transitive affect module consumers?
explanation: A module that reads the requiring module also reads the transitively required dependency, exposing an API dependency relationship.

questions.title: Why use qualified exports?
explanation: They expose a package only to named friend modules, limiting compile-time and runtime access while preserving selected integration.

questions.title: What is a ModuleLayer useful for?
explanation: It creates additional resolved module configurations with controlled class loaders, useful for isolated plugin or container-like architectures.

questions.title: What does a multi-release JAR provide?
explanation: It can package version-specific class implementations under a standard layout while presenting base classes to older runtimes.

questions.title: Why can Class.forName initialize a class unexpectedly?
explanation: The common overload loads and initializes the class, so static code runs; another overload lets callers choose initialization explicitly.

code.snippet: Class<?> type = Class.forName("com.example.Plugin", false, loader);

questions.title: What is the difference between young and old generation pressure?
explanation: Short-lived allocation drives young collections, while retained live data and promotion pressure old regions and can lead to longer global work.

questions.title: Why can an oversized heap increase operational risk?
explanation: It consumes memory headroom and may lengthen recovery or full-collection work; sizing must balance live set, allocation, pause, and container limits.

questions.title: What does a GC pause percentile reveal that an average hides?
explanation: Percentiles expose tail latency experienced by slower requests, while an average can conceal rare but damaging long pauses.

questions.title: How can direct byte buffers cause memory pressure outside the Java heap?
explanation: Their native storage is not counted as ordinary heap objects, so heap graphs alone can miss large direct-memory retention.

questions.title: What is metaspace used for?
explanation: Metaspace stores class metadata in native memory; excessive class loading or loader retention can grow it independently of the Java heap.

questions.title: How does class-data sharing improve startup?
explanation: A preprocessed archive lets JVM instances map shared class metadata, reducing startup work and some memory footprint.

questions.title: What does escape analysis enable?
explanation: When the JIT proves an object does not escape, it may eliminate allocation, scalar-replace fields, or remove synchronization.

questions.title: Why must JVM benchmarks include warm-up and forks?
explanation: Warm-up permits adaptive compilation, while separate forks reduce contamination from prior profiles, heap state, and compiled code.

questions.title: How should a thread dump be interpreted?
explanation: Look for repeated blocked or waiting stacks, lock ownership, pool saturation, and cycles across several time-separated dumps rather than one isolated snapshot.

questions.title: What evidence does this native-memory command provide?
explanation: Native Memory Tracking summarizes JVM native allocations by subsystem, helping distinguish heap issues from metaspace, code cache, threads, or arenas.

code.snippet: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary

questions.title: When should a heap dump be captured?
explanation: Capture near the problematic state with enough disk and privacy controls, then inspect dominators and retention paths rather than only object counts.

questions.title: What can a custom Java Flight Recorder event add?
explanation: It records domain timings and attributes beside JVM events, enabling correlation between business operations, allocation, I/O, locks, and pauses.

questions.title: Why is unified JVM logging useful?
explanation: A consistent tag, level, and output configuration exposes GC, class loading, safepoints, and other subsystems without separate legacy flags.

questions.title: What does jcmd offer during live diagnosis?
explanation: It sends supported diagnostic commands to a JVM for recordings, thread information, heap data, flags, and native-memory summaries.

questions.title: How does jstack differ from Java Flight Recorder?
explanation: jstack gives a point-in-time thread snapshot; JFR records time-correlated events and samples over an interval with broader context.

questions.title: What can javap reveal?
explanation: It disassembles class files to show descriptors, bytecode, constants, and generated members such as bridges, helping connect source to JVM behavior.

questions.title: Why use jlink for a deployment image?
explanation: It assembles a runtime containing selected modules and dependencies, reducing distribution size and making the runtime contents explicit.

questions.title: What does jpackage add beyond jlink?
explanation: It creates platform-specific application packages and launchers, optionally using a custom runtime image, for installable desktop or service distribution.

questions.title: How should jdeps results be interpreted for reflection-heavy code?
explanation: Static analysis finds bytecode dependencies but may miss names loaded from configuration or reflection, so runtime tests must supplement it.

questions.title: What does this javap option show?
explanation: The command prints private members and bytecode instructions, useful for inspecting compiler-generated implementation details.

code.snippet: javap -p -c com.example.OrderService

questions.title: What safety model does the Foreign Function and Memory API use?
explanation: Memory segments have explicit bounds, lifetime, and thread-access rules, while linker descriptors make native call shapes explicit.

questions.title: Why is an Arena important for foreign memory?
explanation: It controls the lifetime of one or more segments so native memory can be released deterministically as a group.

questions.title: What risk remains when calling native code through the FFM API?
explanation: Incorrect layouts, descriptors, addresses, or native behavior can still corrupt memory or crash the process despite safer Java-side abstractions.

questions.title: How does a memory layout describe native data?
explanation: It models sizes, alignment, ordering, and nested fields so access handles can target structured off-heap data predictably.

questions.title: When should an API return an interface instead of a concrete collection?
explanation: An interface exposes required behavior while preserving implementation freedom, but the contract must still state mutability, ordering, nulls, and concurrency.

questions.title: Why should public APIs validate arguments at their boundary?
explanation: Early validation produces clear failures before state changes or downstream work, protecting invariants and reducing ambiguous error propagation.

source.title: Secure Coding Guidelines for Java SE

questions.title: How should equality be designed for inheritance?
explanation: Because equals must remain symmetric and transitive, value equality across extensible subclasses is fragile; final value types or composition simplify the contract.

questions.title: Why should toString avoid secrets and expensive side effects?
explanation: It is called implicitly by logs and debuggers, so it should be safe, bounded, stable enough for diagnostics, and free of credentials or personal data.

questions.title: What makes a Java API interruption-friendly?
explanation: Blocking methods declare or propagate interruption, cleanup preserves invariants, and code does not swallow the flag before a cancellation boundary can observe it.

questions.title: What lifetime does this confined arena enforce?
explanation: The native allocation is valid only until the try block closes the arena; later access through the segment fails instead of silently using freed memory.

questions.title: What makes an HTTP method safe?
explanation: A safe method is defined as read-only in its requested semantics, even though logging or billing side effects may occur. Clients and crawlers rely on that contract.

questions.title: How does HTTP idempotency differ from safety?
explanation: Idempotency means repeating the same request has the same intended effect as one request; a method may change state yet still be idempotent.

questions.title: When should an API return 201 Created instead of 200 OK?
explanation: Use 201 when the request creates a resource, normally with a Location header identifying it; 200 fits a successful response whose semantics are not specifically resource creation.

questions.title: What is the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
explanation: 401 indicates missing or invalid authentication and carries an authentication challenge; 403 means the server understood the request but refuses to authorize it.

questions.title: When is 409 Conflict more suitable than 422 Unprocessable Content?
explanation: 409 identifies a conflict with current resource state, while 422 says the representation is syntactically understood but its instructions cannot be processed.

questions.title: Why should a DELETE endpoint define repeat-request behavior?
explanation: DELETE is idempotent at the semantic level, but later responses may differ. The contract should state whether an absent resource returns 204, 404, or another result.

questions.title: How do ETag and If-Match prevent lost updates?
explanation: A client sends the version it edited; the server changes state only if the current entity tag still matches, otherwise returning a precondition failure.

questions.title: What does content negotiation add to an API?
explanation: Request headers describe acceptable representations and server responses select one, with Vary helping caches distinguish variants.

questions.title: Why should request bodies on GET be avoided for general APIs?
explanation: HTTP assigns no generally defined semantics to GET content and intermediaries may reject or ignore it, reducing interoperability and cache predictability.

questions.title: What does this conditional update response mean?
explanation: A 412 response means the If-Match precondition failed, so the client should fetch current state and reconcile instead of overwriting it.

code.snippet:
PUT /orders/42 HTTP/1.1
If-Match: "v7"
Content-Type: application/json

{"status":"approved"}

HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed

questions.title: Why is cursor pagination safer than offset pagination for changing data?
explanation: A stable cursor continues from an ordered key, reducing duplicates and gaps caused by inserts or deletes before an offset.

questions.title: What properties should a pagination cursor have?
explanation: It should be opaque to clients, tamper-resistant when needed, tied to a deterministic sort, and capable of representing a unique continuation position.

questions.title: How should an API evolve an enum without breaking clients?
explanation: Clients should tolerate unknown future values where possible, and servers should avoid reusing meanings; the schema and compatibility policy must state extensibility.

questions.title: When is URL versioning preferable to header versioning?
explanation: URL versions are visible and easy to route and document, while header versions keep resource URLs stable but add tooling and caching complexity.

questions.title: Why should PATCH semantics be explicitly documented?
explanation: PATCH formats differ in operation, null handling, conflicts, and idempotency. A media type and concurrency contract prevent ambiguous partial updates.

questions.title: What does an idempotency key protect on a POST endpoint?
explanation: The server associates a client-generated key with the operation outcome so retries return the prior result rather than repeat an external effect.

source.title: OWASP Business Logic Security Cheat Sheet

questions.title: How should bulk API partial failures be represented?
explanation: Define whether the batch is atomic or per-item, return a stable result for every item, and make retry behavior unambiguous to avoid duplicate work.

questions.title: Why should API field absence differ from explicit null?
explanation: Absence can mean leave unchanged or use a default, while null can mean clear the value; collapsing them makes updates and validation ambiguous.

questions.title: What does RFC 9457 standardize for API errors?
explanation: It defines a problem-details object with type, status, title, detail, instance, and extension members so machines and humans receive consistent errors.

source.title: RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs

questions.title: What is wrong with this unbounded collection endpoint?
explanation: It has no stable order or response-size bound, so data growth can increase latency and memory without limit; add deterministic pagination and maximum page size.

code.snippet:
GET /api/orders HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK

[ /* every order in the database */ ]

questions.title: Why must authorization be checked on every object access?
explanation: Authentication alone does not prove ownership or permission for a requested identifier; the server must enforce object-level policy for each operation.

questions.title: What is the difference between role-based and attribute-based access control?
explanation: RBAC grants permissions through roles, while ABAC evaluates subject, resource, action, and context attributes for finer-grained decisions.

questions.title: Why is deny-by-default important in backend authorization?
explanation: New routes, actions, or resources remain inaccessible until policy explicitly allows them, reducing exposure from omissions.

questions.title: Where should JWT validation occur?
explanation: Every trust boundary accepting the token must verify its signature, issuer, audience, time constraints, and allowed algorithms before using claims.

questions.title: Why should a server not trust an algorithm declared only by a JWT header?
explanation: An attacker controls the header; the verifier must enforce a configured algorithm allowlist and the correct key type.

questions.title: How do CORS and server-side authorization differ?
explanation: CORS limits which browser origins can read responses, while authorization determines whether any client may perform the action; non-browser clients ignore CORS.

questions.title: When is CSRF protection needed for an API?
explanation: It is needed when browsers automatically attach credentials such as cookies; same-site settings, origin checks, and anti-CSRF tokens can bind intent.

questions.title: Why should rate limits distinguish identity and endpoint cost?
explanation: One global request count treats cheap and expensive work alike and can be evaded across identities; limits should reflect principals, operations, and resource cost.

questions.title: How should secrets be supplied to a backend service?
explanation: Inject them from a managed secret source at runtime, restrict access, rotate them, and keep them out of source, logs, images, and client-delivered configuration.

questions.title: What vulnerability exists in this ownership check?
explanation: The handler loads by user-supplied ID without constraining the query by the authenticated owner, enabling insecure direct object access.

questions.title: What does atomicity guarantee in a database transaction?
explanation: All transaction changes commit together or none do, preventing callers from observing a partially applied business operation.

questions.title: How do read committed and repeatable read differ?
explanation: Read committed gives each statement a fresh committed snapshot, while PostgreSQL repeatable read keeps a transaction snapshot and rejects certain conflicting updates.

questions.title: What anomaly does serializable isolation prevent?
explanation: It ensures committed transactions have an outcome equivalent to some serial order, potentially aborting transactions that must be retried.

questions.title: Why must serializable transaction failures be retried as a whole?
explanation: The database rejects an execution whose combined reads and writes are unsafe; retrying only the last statement does not recreate a valid transaction view.

questions.title: When should SELECT FOR UPDATE be used?
explanation: Use it when a transaction must lock selected rows before a dependent update, while keeping lock scope and transaction duration small.

source.title: OWASP Business Logic Security Cheat Sheet

questions.title: How can a conditional update enforce a business invariant?
explanation: Put the invariant in the WHERE clause and check affected rows, making the check and mutation one atomic database statement.

source.title: OWASP Business Logic Security Cheat Sheet

questions.title: Why should external network calls usually not occur inside a database transaction?
explanation: They extend lock time and may fail independently, increasing contention and creating ambiguous outcomes across systems.

questions.title: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve?
explanation: It commits domain changes and an outbound event record together, then publishes asynchronously, avoiding a gap between database commit and message send.

questions.title: How should transaction boundaries align with business operations?
explanation: A boundary should protect one consistency unit, remaining short while including every database change needed to preserve its invariants.

questions.title: Why can this balance check race?
explanation: Two transactions can both read the same balance before either subtracts. A conditional update, row lock, or serializable transaction makes the decision atomic.

source.title: OWASP Business Logic Security Cheat Sheet

questions.title: How does a composite index column order affect queries?
explanation: Leading columns determine which equality, range, ordering, and prefix predicates can efficiently use the index.

questions.title: Why can an index speed reads but slow writes?
explanation: Each insert, delete, or indexed-column update must maintain the index and generate storage and logging work.

questions.title: What is a covering index?
explanation: It contains all columns needed by a query so the engine may answer from the index, subject to visibility and planner decisions.

questions.title: When is a partial index useful?
explanation: It indexes only rows matching a predicate, reducing size and update work for queries that repeatedly target that subset.

questions.title: Why can applying a function to an indexed column prevent index use?
explanation: A normal index stores the raw expression value; an unmatched transformation may require scanning unless an expression index or equivalent predicate exists.

questions.title: What should be inspected in EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
explanation: Compare estimated and actual rows, scan types, loops, sort or hash spills, buffer activity, and total timing under representative parameters.

questions.title: Why are foreign-key indexes often still needed?
explanation: A foreign key enforces integrity but does not automatically guarantee the child-side index needed for joins, parent deletes, and updates.

questions.title: How should a zero-downtime column migration be staged?
explanation: Add a compatible nullable or defaulted shape, deploy dual-compatible code, backfill in bounded batches, enforce constraints, then remove the old shape later.

questions.title: Why should schema migrations be forward-only in production?
explanation: Applied data transformations may not be safely reversible; a new corrective migration preserves an auditable sequence and avoids rewriting history.

questions.title: What does this query plan warning suggest?
explanation: A sequential scan with a large row estimate may be correct, but for selective filters it prompts checking statistics, predicates, and a suitable index.

code.snippet:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';

questions.title: What is the cache-aside pattern?
explanation: The application reads the cache first, loads from the source on a miss, and then populates the cache; writes require a deliberate invalidation strategy.

questions.title: Why is cache invalidation harder than cache population?
explanation: Multiple writers, races, failures, and replicas can leave stale values, so ownership, ordering, TTLs, and acceptable staleness must be defined.

questions.title: How does write-through differ from write-behind caching?
explanation: Write-through updates the source synchronously with the cache, while write-behind queues persistence later and risks loss or reordering on failure.

questions.title: What is a cache stampede?
explanation: Many requests miss or expire the same hot key simultaneously and overload the source; request coalescing, jitter, or stale serving can reduce it.

questions.title: Why add jitter to cache TTLs?
explanation: Randomizing expiration spreads refresh work over time instead of allowing many related keys to expire at one instant.

questions.title: When is negative caching appropriate?
explanation: Caching a not-found or failure result can protect the source from repeated misses, but requires a short policy that does not hide newly created data too long.

questions.title: What does stale-while-revalidate achieve?
explanation: A cache may serve a stale response within a defined window while refreshing asynchronously, improving latency at the cost of bounded staleness.

questions.title: Why must private responses be handled carefully by shared caches?
explanation: User-specific content must not be reused for another user; cache directives and key design must prevent cross-account data exposure.

questions.title: How should cache keys be designed?
explanation: Include every request dimension that changes the result, normalize representation safely, namespace versions, and avoid raw sensitive data.

questions.title: What problem exists in this cache lookup?
explanation: The key omits the authenticated tenant, so identical order IDs across tenants can expose one tenant's cached data to another.

questions.title: What does at-least-once message delivery require from consumers?
explanation: A message can be delivered again after failures, so handlers must deduplicate or make each state transition idempotent.

questions.title: Why is exactly-once an end-to-end property rather than only a broker setting?
explanation: Broker transactions cannot automatically make databases, emails, payments, and external APIs participate in the same atomic outcome.

questions.title: How do consumer groups scale a partitioned log?
explanation: Partitions are assigned among group members so each partition has one active consumer in the group while members process partitions in parallel.

questions.title: Why does partition-key choice matter?
explanation: It controls ordering scope, load distribution, and locality; a hot key can bottleneck one partition while random keys may destroy needed ordering.

questions.title: When should an event carry a schema version?
explanation: Versioning lets consumers interpret evolving payloads and supports compatibility checks without guessing fields from deployment timing.

questions.title: What is a dead-letter queue for?
explanation: It isolates messages that cannot be processed after policy limits, preserving evidence for diagnosis and controlled replay rather than infinite retry.

questions.title: How should poison-message retries be bounded?
explanation: Classify permanent versus transient failures, use delayed backoff, cap attempts, and route exhausted work with diagnostic context.

questions.title: What does backpressure mean in a messaging pipeline?
explanation: Downstream capacity limits must propagate upstream through bounded queues, flow control, or rejection so memory and latency do not grow without bound.

questions.title: Why should event consumers tolerate unknown fields?
explanation: Forward-compatible readers can continue when producers add optional data, while strict rejection turns harmless evolution into coordinated downtime.

questions.title: What is unsafe about committing this offset first?
explanation: A crash after committing but before the database update loses the event. Commit only after durable processing or use a coordinated idempotent design.

code.snippet:
await consumer.commitOffsets(message);
await database.applyOrderEvent(message.value);

questions.title: Why should every outbound call have a timeout?
explanation: Without a deadline, stalled dependencies retain connections, threads, memory, and request capacity indefinitely.

questions.title: How should retry backoff be designed?
explanation: Use exponential growth, jitter, a deadline, and a capped attempt budget, retrying only transient and safe operations.

questions.title: What does a circuit breaker accomplish?
explanation: After repeated failures it fails fast for a recovery interval, protecting capacity and giving a dependency time to recover.

questions.title: How does a bulkhead limit failure spread?
explanation: Separate pools, queues, or concurrency limits keep one saturated dependency or workload from consuming all service resources.

questions.title: When should a service shed load?
explanation: Reject work early when capacity or latency budgets are exhausted, prioritizing critical traffic rather than letting every request time out slowly.

questions.title: Why must a retry budget consider the whole request graph?
explanation: Retries multiply across layers and fan-out calls, so independent policies can create an exponential traffic surge during failure.

questions.title: What is graceful degradation?
explanation: The service preserves a useful core response while disabling optional work when dependencies or capacity are impaired.

questions.title: How should a bounded worker queue be sized?
explanation: Base it on arrival bursts, service rate, memory per item, and latency objectives; a larger queue can merely hide overload and increase delay.

questions.title: What is head-of-line blocking?
explanation: A slow item at the front of a shared queue or connection delays unrelated fast work behind it, motivating isolation or multiplexing.

questions.title: Why is this retry loop dangerous?
explanation: It retries immediately without a limit, deadline, jitter, or error classification, amplifying a dependency outage and never releasing the request.

questions.title: How do logs, metrics, and traces complement each other?
explanation: Logs capture discrete context, metrics summarize trends and alerts, and traces follow request paths and latency across service boundaries.

questions.title: What makes a log entry structured?
explanation: It records stable typed fields such as timestamp, severity, operation, trace ID, and outcome rather than embedding everything in prose.

questions.title: Why should request correlation IDs cross service boundaries?
explanation: They connect related records across hops when tracing is incomplete, while each service should still generate safe identifiers when none arrive.

questions.title: What is metric cardinality and why can it be dangerous?
explanation: Each label combination creates a time series; unbounded values such as user IDs or URLs can overwhelm monitoring storage and query systems.

questions.title: How does a service-level objective differ from an alert threshold?
explanation: An SLO states the desired reliability over a window, while alerts should signal meaningful error-budget burn or required operator action.

questions.title: What is an error budget?
explanation: It is the allowed unreliability implied by an SLO, enabling teams to balance feature velocity against reliability risk.

questions.title: Why are latency percentiles more useful than averages?
explanation: They reveal tail behavior experienced by slow requests; a healthy average can coexist with unacceptable p95 or p99 latency.

questions.title: What should a health endpoint report?
explanation: It should expose narrowly defined liveness or readiness without leaking secrets, blocking on every dependency, or pretending partial failure is full health.

questions.title: How should trace sampling be chosen?
explanation: Balance cost with diagnostic value, retaining rare errors and high-latency paths through tail or policy-aware sampling where infrastructure supports it.

questions.title: What observability issue does this metric label create?
explanation: Using raw user IDs creates effectively unbounded cardinality. Aggregate by bounded dimensions and put user-specific detail in controlled logs or traces.

questions.title: How do liveness and readiness probes differ?
explanation: Liveness decides whether to restart a stuck process; readiness decides whether it should receive traffic while starting, draining, or dependency-impaired.

questions.title: Why must graceful shutdown stop accepting new work before exiting?
explanation: Draining first lets in-flight requests and messages finish or transfer safely instead of being cut off during deployment.

questions.title: What does configuration parity across environments prevent?
explanation: Keeping configuration mechanisms consistent reduces production-only behavior, while values such as endpoints and credentials remain environment-specific.

questions.title: Why should deployment artifacts be immutable?
explanation: The same tested artifact moves between environments, preventing rebuild drift and making rollback and provenance reliable.

questions.title: How does a contract test differ from an end-to-end test?
explanation: A contract test checks one consumer-provider interface quickly, while an end-to-end test validates a deployed user path across integrated components.

questions.title: What should an integration test isolate?
explanation: It should exercise real boundaries such as database or broker behavior while controlling unrelated external systems for deterministic evidence.

questions.title: Why should load tests use representative data distributions?
explanation: Uniform synthetic data misses hot keys, skewed payloads, cache behavior, query plans, and contention that dominate production performance.

questions.title: What is the purpose of chaos testing?
explanation: It verifies that defined failure controls, recovery, and observability work under injected faults, within explicit blast-radius and rollback safeguards.

questions.title: How should globally unique IDs be selected?
explanation: Choose based on collision bounds, ordering leakage, index locality, generation coordination, and interoperability rather than assuming one format fits all systems.

questions.title: What rollout risk does this readiness check create?
explanation: Tying readiness to every optional dependency can remove all instances during one downstream outage, turning partial degradation into total unavailability.
